[h1]Absolute waste of potential[/h1] I'll start saying that I play poker online. I know a little bit about trading methods and card counting. I really love probability and I'm familiar with many of its concepts. [h2] There is no reason for there to be a cap to any of the upgrades [/h2] My first impression is that the game is meant to portray that while short-term luck exists, the way probabilities work is long term, which means that you could get lucky and end the game immediately or not at all. The thing is that any probability will end up happening given an infinite number of trials, even getting 10,000 heads in a row will happen if you just keep flipping (of course this is considering you are also immortal), you can search the [b]Borel–Cantelli lemma[/b] if you aren't convinced. The probability of getting ten heads in a row with a 60% winrate is (0.60)^10 ≈ 0.6% There is literally no challenge involved, the game claims that it could be that you never win, but the truth is that if you keep flipping it's almost impossible that you don't win, the whole gimmick of idle games is to become overpowered and winning more easily, so if I'm going to turn off my brain pushing a damn button then at least give me a 99% chance of hitting heads so that I can finish the game quicker. It doesn't even change the core of the game because technically you could still spend a lifetime with a 99% winrate and never win. [h2] The economy is extremely slow [/h2] In the early game it is understandable, maybe it's trying to showcase how bad the starter coin is, and that is why the first upgrades take a little bit of time. But then, because the game caps the items it makes it so that you are only getting money if you are lucky enough to hit a streak of heads and because you can only flip once every second it takes a long time to be able to actually get the 60% coin. So you actually only play like the first 15 minutes of the game waiting for upgrades to gain something unique and then you realize that that's the whole game, just pushing a button and waiting to get lucky. [h2] This game fails at teaching probabilities and at being fun [/h2] Probabilities are a complicated subject. If they weren't casinos wouldn't exist. I just don't understand the purpose of this game. Telling players that probabilities work in the long term? Making the achievements for the endings look cute? The only challenge this game has is your patience, it is 30 minutes of maxing out the upgrades and then just waiting to end the game while you look at your phone. [h2] Ways to make the game better [/h2] [h3] Goal [/h3] Embrace the fact that the game would be a lot more fun if you feel you are getting closer to the goal. One way to do this could be to make the goal getting 100 heads in a row and exponentially increasing the probability of getting heads, this would pair well with the fact that streaks are what give you the most money. Make the first coin even worse (like a 10% chance), leave the goal of getting 10 heads in a row but increase the money production every time the coin does land on heads. Make the coin start incredibly slow but with a really high chance to get heads and focus the upgrades around the speed, then make the goal be getting to a million dollars or something. [h3] Upgrades[/h3] Don't cap the upgrades, it would be cool to get to the realization that at some point you should prioritize speed of the coin over the multiplier, or make a coin that prioritizes the probability over the speed. Just let the player get closer to the goal instead of capping everything and saying "Well good luck for the next hour until you get lucky" [h3] Showcasing probability concepts [/h3] What about getting an unlucky bonus if you get tails a certain amount of times in a row? What if every time you get tails you lose some money and explain the [b]Kelly Criterion[/b] while the player tries not to go bankrupt What if you could make side bets on the amount of times you will get heads or tails in the next 20 flips, and use that to explain variance in the context of a profitable bet? [h2] Conclusion[/h2] This game makes me mad, it had a lot of traction and it looked like a really cool concept with a lot of room to grow but the way it is right now the gameplay is just pushing a button and waiting, waiting, and waiting. If you want to experience this without wasting any money then grab a coin and flip it until you get heads 10 times in a row. That's all there is to it.

For context, I have a background in mathematics and statistics: This game claims to be one thing, and that is an accurate model of flipping a coin with a given probability. It says this more than once in each playthrough, and doesn't claim to be much else aside. You flip the coin until you get nine heads in a row, then you flip it a tenth time - here, it can land on tails, but if it would land on heads it instead selects one of a number of endings, each with a different "probability" of occurring. I have criticisms of Unfair Flips as a game, most notably how shallow the progression is - you quickly come to a point where clicking or pressing to flip the coin is the only thing left to do, and even 9 heads in a row doesn't generate enough money to improve your claimed odds of getting heads. But my primary criticism is of what it claims to be, and be doing: I've played through the game more times than any one person should, and I quickly noticed that I was getting unusually long strings of tails, though I initially brushed it off as randomness, but it was happening consistently on my runs, and so I decided to start tracking the longest runs of heads and tails at each probability, and just now had the following run: 35%: 3H (4.29%), 15T (0.16%) 40%: 4H (2.56%), 13T (0.13%) 45%: 6H (0.83%), 7T (1.52%) 50%: 5H (3.13%), 8T (0.39%) 55%: 9H (0.46%), 8T (0.17%) for the 45% round, I got seven tails immediately, a heads, a tails, and then six heads before landing a final tails - which gave me enough money to upgrade the probability of my coin landing on heads, so that round only had 16 flips which isn't a reasonably large sample size for anything. At the 55% round, when I got 9 heads in a row the game ended - in both cases, there is some selection bias in the favour of long runs of heads. In the other rounds, you can see that the likelihood of seeing such a long run of tails in a row is some order of magnitude lower than the odds of the longest run of heads I saw - and each of those rounds also had a selection bias for heads, because the probability can only change when you've seen enough heads (or a long enough run of heads) to afford the probability upgrade, so typically you stop testing after a long run of heads, which favours you seeing a statistically unlikely run of heads more so than it does for runs of tails. I've only tracked the runs for one round of the game, but I was noticing this pattern often in previous runs, and this last run is consistent with what I've seen previously - which is the opposite of what you'd expect to see when there's an implicit bias for runs of heads when you're playing this as a clicker game. The sample size for an individual player is always going to be small, but this was very noticeable very early on. In a similar vein: that last run was my thirteenth run of the game, and my tenth time getting the "splode" ending (claimed to be 30% likely) after flipping nine heads. Stattrek helpfully tells me that, if you were to play 13 rounds of this game, the odds of getting an ending with 30% likelihood ten or more times is a whopping 0.07%. Ultimately, I wouldn't recommend this as a game for it's weak progression system, but I can't recommend this as a product at all for two reasons: firstly, because I don't think it accurately models what it claims to; and secondly, because as much as I could request a refund for the £1.69 I spent on this game, there is no refunding your time.

A game more interesting to think about than it is to play. You'll have plenty of time to think about the game, as its economy fairly quickly runs out of most upgrades and becomes a waiting game for 8x heads in a row to get any meaningful amount of money. The game is fine if you are looking for a fidget toy, but as a clicker game it's indulgence in its highly ergodic economy system wears thin fairly quickly. It appears that the devs sought out to make precisely this kind of experience, so they should commend themselves for doing so and for the beautiful artwork and soundscape. But for the average player, there just isn't much here.

I've never written a negative review before and I never thought I would. I prefer to be a generally positive person and don't like being critical, but I feel like I have an obligation to save others the frustration I experienced. Unfair Flips is just a bad experience. At first it was maybe a little fun, but it quickly became a chore. There are only 4 types of upgrades you can buy and it doesn't take long to max out 3 of the 4. Then there are no more meaningful choices to be made and the game just gets really really boring. The worst part is that the final upgrade of flip chance only gets you to 60% heads, which means ten heads in a row is worse than a 1 in 165 chance. Just clicking over and over again (and not even as fast as you can - you are still limited to about once a second) is really boring and really frustrating. It's not fun at all anymore. Imagine playing a solo dice game where you roll percentile dice over and over waiting for a roll of 100. Super boring, right? This is worse. It took me maybe half an hour to get to the point where I only had 1 upgrade category left, and even when that got maxed out about half an hour later, I still had almost half an hour of more of pointless flipping to do before I finally got to *one* of the random endings. Turns out, there are five ways for it to end and the game randomly gives you one when you are supposed to have gotten the 10th heads. Only 10% of the time will it actually give you a 10th head. Collecting all the endings would be ridiculously boring and even getting to one ending was completely unsatisfying. I would not recommend this game to anyone, even if it were offered for free. If you want the random clicking experience, but one that is actually fun and satisfying, try One More 6ix instead.

At first I thought: "Wow, this is simple." Then four hours passed and I've reached new levels of insanity. I fear I've grown to believe there is more to this game than probability. After hours of flipping this coin, I've convinced myself there is a timing- a rhythm the coin seems to like. I FLIP. Again and again. Every flip, I've grown increasingly more suspicious. Is this really only probability? I find myself at the edge of my seat, am I destined for failure? Is this some sick and twisted game? No- over time, I've become addicted to the chase. Every small frail success fuels my motivation. A 20% chance of landing on heads? Easy. I welcome a challenge.

For a very cheap game, the idea is interesting and the gameplay at first is very cool. You basically are just flipping a coin with very unfair odds (which is more fun than it sounds) but when the odds rarely do favor you, you get some money, after getting lucky a few times you can start buying upgrades to increase money generation or increase the chances of getting lucky heads on the coin. Once you reach enough upgrades (or get astronomically lucky) you get to 9 heads in a row and the game selects one from 5 different endings each with their own odds(30%/20%/20%/20%/10%) and you need to flip the coin to see which ending you got. And here is the big problem, after that you SHOULD just need to get 9 heads in a row again to reach an ending, again... but for absolutely no reason, after you get an ending the game resets your whole progress instantly. The premisse of the game is that odds are odds and you can't manipulate them, if you have unfair or "even" odds (50%) the only way to achieve a skewed goal is to have time and patience, and technically you statistically can never achieve the goal if you get mega unlucky and be stuck in it forever. HOWEVER the game resetting your whole progress after an ending, is just to make you waste more time, and defeats the purpose of "bad odds take time" because this isn't bad odds, the game reset your progress just because. And speaking from a game design perspective, artificially prolonging the game for no reason (or at least not a good one) IS a bad game design. Let's talk odds, took me roughly 1 hour to get my first ending, so assuming i get as lucky everytime it's roughly 1 hour to reach an ending everytime by doing a lame task (because after getting your progress reset, all the fun in the game gets sucked out of you) and so with 5 endings it takes 5h to beat the game minimum when it could have been done much quicker and more fun. But also no guarantee i'll see a new ending so i might just get the same ending everytime, and waste time, which WOULD be on par with the premisse of "you can't manipulate odds, it takes time" but again you are not wasting time because of the bad odds themselves, you are wasting time because the progress gets reset JUST to extend playtime and no other reason. If you have a few spare change to spend and has a LOT of time to waste and love doing a boring menial task for no reason other than a weird self fullfillment, go ahead and buy it. Otherwise i can't recommend this
